title: Designing healthcare for people and planet: What if every act of care also cared for the planet?
acknowledgements: Aws Almukhtar, Daniella Watson, Jessica Newberry Le Vay, Leila Shepherd, Matt Harrison, and Natalia Kurek
short_description: This blog explores how healthcare can be designed to reduce its environmental impact, setting out six areas where design can help the NHS cut waste and emissions while improving care.
lay_summary:
Healthcare contributes to climate change, but it can also be part of the solution. In the UK, the NHS accounts for around 4 to 5 per cent of the country's total carbon emissions. At the same time, climate change is making people ill through heatwaves, floods and worsening air quality. This creates a double challenge: health systems need to reduce their own environmental footprint while also preparing for rising demand.

This blog, written by Helix Centre designers Sophie Horrocks and Tori Simpson, sets out six areas where design can help. These are: reducing clinical waste, making care pathways more sustainable, greening digital health technologies, designing hospital buildings for a low-carbon future, shifting care into communities, and embedding sustainability into policy and everyday practice.

For each area, the authors describe the problem, share examples of work already underway, and point to sessions at the World Design Congress where these ideas were being explored further. The examples range from a behavioural "nudge" tested by Helix to reduce unnecessary glove use on hospital wards (which led to an 11 per cent improvement in hand hygiene compliance), to the NHS's first zero-emissions ambulance being trialled in the West Midlands, to solar panels at Milton Keynes University Hospital generating around 8 per cent of the site's electricity.

The blog also highlights tensions that need to be navigated. For example, digital tools can cut travel and improve efficiency, but data centres use large amounts of energy and water. Reusable medical equipment can reduce waste, but sterilising it is sometimes as carbon-intensive as replacing it. And while moving care into communities can lower emissions, it must be done in ways that do not leave people behind.

The authors argue that sustainability should not feel like an extra burden for already stretched health services. Instead, there are "win-wins" to be found, where greener choices also improve care, save money, or support staff wellbeing. They invite designers, clinicians and partners to join the conversation and help shape healthcare that protects both people and the planet.

title: Monitoring night-time safety in households with dementia using ambient sensing technologies: a rule-based decision algorithm
authors: Alina-Irina Serban, Sophie Horrocks, Chloe Walsh, Matthew Harrison, Eyal Soreq, Amer Marzuki, Mark Woodbridge, Ramin Nilforooshan, Rafael A Calvo, David J Sharp
short_description: Researchers developed and tested a system that uses sensors in the home to detect when a person with dementia leaves the house or opens a door at night, so that family carers can be alerted to potential safety risks.
lay_summary:
Wandering at night is common among people living with dementia, affecting around 6 in 10 people as the condition progresses. It can put people at risk of falls, getting lost, or being outside in unsafe conditions, and it adds to the strain on family members and carers. Despite how often it happens, there are few reliable tools to help spot these risks early.

A team led by the UK Dementia Research Institute's Care Research and Technology centre, with design expertise from the Helix Centre, developed a monitoring system to address this. The system uses sensors placed around the home: motion detectors, door sensors, and a mat placed under the mattress that tracks whether someone is in bed. An automated algorithm analyses the data from these sensors to identify patterns that might signal a safety concern, such as leaving the house during the night or leaving a door open.

The algorithm was tested in stages, including trials in a living lab (a test home set up for research), computer simulations, and real-world use. The main validation involved 94 households monitored over 365 nights, totalling nearly 300,000 hours of data. In 33 of those households, at least one night-time safety alert was triggered. Across all households, the system generated 200 alerts over 142 nights. When someone did go out at night, they were outside for an average of 2 hours and 40 minutes per event.

Of the alerts, about 9 in 10 were confirmed as genuine night-time outings. Around 15% of those turned out to be routine activities rather than risky events, which is a useful reminder that not every alert means something is wrong.

This was a validation study, not a trial of whether the system improves outcomes for people with dementia or their carers. The authors note that the system has the potential to improve safety and reduce carer burden, but further research would be needed to test that in practice. The study also relied on sensor data rather than direct observation, so some events may have been missed or misclassified.
